Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 84, verse 1–5 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿When the sky is split asunder (1) and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to (2). And when the earth is stretched out (3) and casts forth what is within it and empties itself (4) and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to (5).﴾

God, exalted is He, says: when the sky is split and torn apart, so that it becomes gates.

* *

As for His words, ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾:
It means: the heavens, in their splitting and cleaving, listen to their Lord and obey Him in His command to them. The Arabs say: "adhina lak fi hadha al-amr adhanan," meaning: "he listened to you," and from this is the report transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ: "God has not listened to anything as He listens to a Prophet who chants the Qur'an" (ma adhina Allahu li-shay'in ka-adhanihi li-nabiyyin yataghanna bil-Qur'an), meaning: God has not listened to anything as He listens to a Prophet who chants the Qur'an. And from it is the verse of the poet:
Deaf when they hear good spoken of me, ...
but when evil is mentioned of me in their presence, they listen (adhinu).[[The report 168 – this isnad is among the most frequently recurring isnads in the tafsir of al-Tabari, if not the most frequent; it is hardly possible for the interpretation of any verse to be free of a narration with this isnad. Al-Tabari himself expressed doubt about it in (p. 121 Bulaq, line 28 and following), when he mentioned the report from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas with this isnad, saying: "If that is sound – and I do not know it to be sound, since its isnad is doubtful to me..." He did not explain the cause of his doubt regarding its isnad, and despite his doubt he narrated through it extensively, yet he never made it a proof.

However, I see it as an isnad requiring careful investigation. The scholars of hadith have spoken about it and about some of its narrators. I have traced what they said and what its investigation calls for, as far as I could, and an opinion has appeared to me which I hope is correct, God willing. My success is only through God:

As for Al-Tabari's teacher, "Musa ibn Harun al-Hamdani": I have not found a biography of him, nor any mention of him in any of the references available to me, except what al-Tabari also narrates from him in his History, more than fifty times in its first and second volumes. There is no need for us to examine his biography in terms of jarh wa ta'dil (criticism and validation), for this tafsir which he narrates from 'Amr ibn Hammad is known among the people of hadith scholarship, and it is merely the transmission of a book, not the transmission of a particular hadith.

"And 'Amr ibn Hammad": he is 'Amr ibn Hammad ibn Talha al-Qannad, and he is sometimes attributed to his grandfather, so it is said 'Amr ibn Talha. He is trustworthy (thiqa). Muslim narrated from him in his Sahih. Ibn Sa'd included his biography in al-Tabaqat 6: 285 and said: "He was trustworthy, God willing." He died in the year 222. Ibn Abi Hatim included his biography in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 3/1/228, and narrated from his father and from Yahya ibn Ma'in that they both said of him: "Sadduq" (truthful).

Asbat ibn Nasr al-Hamdani: he is disputed. Ahmad weakened him, and Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat: 410. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 1/2/53 and did not mention any criticism of him. Ibn Abi Hatim included his biography in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/332 and narrated from Yahya ibn Ma'in who said: "Asbat ibn Nasr is trustworthy." We have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad, in hadith 1286.

Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Karima al-Suddi: he is al-Suddi al-Kabir, a Qurashi by clientage (mawla), client of Zaynab bint Qays ibn Makhrama, from the Banu 'Abd Manaf, as al-Bukhari stated in his two histories: al-Saghir: 141–142, and al-Kabir 1/1/361. He was a Tabi'i. He heard Anas, as al-Bukhari also stated, and narrated from other Companions and from many Tabi'un. He is trustworthy. Muslim narrated from him in his Sahih. Ahmad ibn Hanbal authenticated him, as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/184, and he also narrated from Ahmad who said: "Yahya ibn Ma'in once said to me in the presence of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi: al-Suddi is weak. 'Abd al-Rahman became angry and disliked what he said." In al-Mizan and al-Tahdhib it is said that al-Sha'bi was told: "al-Suddi has been given a portion of knowledge of the Qur'an," and he said: "He has been given a portion of ignorance of the Qur'an!" In my view this statement of al-Sha'bi may be the basis for the words of everyone who spoke about al-Suddi unjustly. For this reason al-Bukhari did not heed this statement of al-Sha'bi and did not narrate it; rather, he narrated in al-Kabir from Musaddad from Yahya who said: "I heard Ibn Abi Khalid say: al-Suddi is more knowledgeable of the Qur'an than al-Sha'bi." He narrated in his two histories from Ibn al-Madini from Yahya, namely al-Qattan, who said: "I have never seen anyone mention al-Suddi except with good, and no one abandoned him." In al-Tahdhib: "al-'Ijli said: trustworthy, a scholar of tafsir, and a transmitter of it." We have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad 807. al-Suddi died in the year 127.

And "al-Suddi": with a damma on the sin and a shadda on the dal (unpointed letters), a nisba to "al-Sudda," which is the door, because he used to sit at the sudda of the mosque in Kufa and sell head-coverings there.

Abu Malik: he is al-Ghifari, whose name is Ghazwan. He is a trustworthy Kufan Tabi'i. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 4/1/108, Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat 6: 206, and Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 3/2/55, and Yahya ibn Ma'in's authentication of him was narrated.

Abu Salih: he is the client of Umm Hani bint Abi Talib, whose name is Badham, and it is said Badhan. He is a trustworthy Tabi'i. We have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad 2030. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 1/2/144, and narrated from Muhammad ibn Bashshar who said: "Ibn Mahdi abandoned the hadith of Abu Salih." Likewise Ibn Abi Hatim narrated in his biography in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/431–432 from Ahmad ibn Hanbal from Ibn Mahdi. But he also narrated from Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan who said: "I have not seen anyone of our companions abandon Abu Salih, the client of Umm Hani, and I have not heard anyone say anything about him; Shu'ba, Za'ida, and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman did not abandon him." He also narrated from Yahya ibn Ma'in who said: "Abu Salih, client of Umm Hani, is not objectionable; but when al-Kalbi narrates from him, he is worth nothing, and when anyone other than al-Kalbi narrates from him, there is nothing objectionable in him, because al-Kalbi narrates it sometimes from his own opinion, sometimes from Abu Salih, and sometimes from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas." He means by this that the criticism concerning what he narrates is in the narration of al-Kalbi, as is evident.

This concludes the first part of this isnad, for in reality it is two or three isnads. The first is this one connected to Ibn 'Abbas.

The second part, or second isnad: "and from Murra al-Hamdani from Ibn Mas'ud." The one who narrates from Murra al-Hamdani is al-Suddi himself.

Murra: he is Ibn Sharahil al-Hamdani al-Kufi, a trustworthy Tabi'i, one of the senior Tabi'un, about whom there is no disagreement among them.

The third part, or third isnad: "and from people among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ."

This too is from al-Suddi's own transmission from some Companions.

So al-Suddi narrates these interpretations of Qur'anic verses: from two Tabi'un from Ibn 'Abbas, from one Tabi'i from Ibn Mas'ud, and from his own transmission from some Companions.

The early imams of the scholars have spoken about this tafsir with these isnads, in a way that may give the impression that it was composed by someone other than al-Suddi among those who narrated from him. However, I have since become certain that it is a book which al-Suddi composed.

Among that is the statement of Ibn Sa'd in the biography of "'Amr ibn Hammad al-Qannad" 6: 285: "companion of the tafsir of Asbat ibn Nasr from al-Suddi." He said in the biography of "Asbat ibn Nasr" 6: 261: "He was a transmitter of al-Suddi, from whom he narrated the tafsir." He said before that in the biography of "al-Suddi" 6: 225: "Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Suddi, the author of the tafsir." He said before that also, in the biography of "Abu Malik al-Ghifari" 6: 206: "Abu Malik al-Ghifari, author of the tafsir, and he had little hadith."

But what indicates that it is a book composed by al-Suddi, in which he gathered the tafsir through these three routes, is the statement of Ahmad ibn Hanbal in al-Tahdhib 1: 314, in the biography of al-Suddi: "He is good in hadith, except that this tafsir which he brings has been given an isnad and he has taxed himself for it." And the statement of al-Hafiz in al-Tahdhib also 1: 315: "al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim and others have transmitted the tafsir of al-Suddi in their tafsirs, dispersed among the surahs, through the route of Asbat ibn Nasr from him."

And the statement of al-Suyuti in al-Itqan 2: 224, as quoted from al-Khalil in al-Irshad: "The tafsir of Isma'il al-Suddi, he narrates it with isnads to Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. The imams narrated from al-Suddi, such as al-Thawri and Shu'ba. But the tafsir which he compiled was narrated by Asbat ibn Nasr, and the scholars did not agree on Asbat. Nevertheless, the most excellent of tafsirs is the tafsir of al-Suddi." Then al-Suyuti said: "The tafsir of al-Suddi, which he referred to, Ibn Jarir narrates much of it through the route of al-Suddi from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murra from Ibn Mas'ud, and [from] people among the Companions. Thus. Ibn Abi Hatim did not narrate anything of it, because he committed himself to bringing out only the most authentic that was transmitted. Al-Hakim brings out some of it in his Mustadrak and authenticates it, but only through the route of Murra from Ibn Mas'ud and the people, alone, without the first route. Ibn Kathir said: this isnad through which al-Suddi narrates things contains strangeness."

The first thing we point out in these statements: the contradiction between the two statements of al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar and al-Suyuti, regarding whether Ibn Abi Hatim brought out the tafsir of al-Suddi dispersed in his tafsir, as al-Tabari did, according to al-Hafiz's transmission, and that he turned away from it, according to al-Suyuti's transmission. I cannot assert anything definite about this, since I have not seen the tafsir of Ibn Abi Hatim. But I lean toward preferring Ibn Hajar's transmission, as he is more careful and precise in transmission than al-Suyuti.

Then al-Suyuti was right about what he transmitted from al-Hakim. For he narrates some of this tafsir in the Mustadrak, with its isnad, to Ahmad ibn Nasr: "Ahmad ibn 'Amr ibn Talha al-Qannad narrated to us, Asbat ibn Nasr narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Suddi, from Murra al-Hamdani, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and from some people among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ." Then he authenticates it on the condition of Muslim, and al-Dhahabi agrees with him in his summary. Such as in the Mustadrak 2: 258, 260, 273, 321.

Al-Hakim is correct in this, for Muslim narrated from all the narrators of this isnad, from 'Amr ibn Hammad ibn Talha al-Qannad to Murra al-Hamdani. He did not narrate from Abu Salih Badham or from Abu Malik al-Ghifari, in the first part of the isnad through which al-Suddi narrated his tafsirs.

As for the words of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal about al-Suddi, "except that this tafsir which he brings has been given an isnad and he has taxed himself for it," he does not mean what might be understood from its apparent meaning: that he fabricated an isnad with no basis; for had that been the case, he would in his view have been a liar and a fabricator of narrations. Rather he means, in my view, and God knows best, that he gathered these tafsirs from his narration from these people: from Abu Malik and Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, from Murra from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some Companions; then he set them all out in detail, on the verses in which some interpretation was reported from this one or that one or those, and gave all of them this isnad, and took pains to present them all in a single line.

That is: he gathered the scattered tafsirs into one book, to which he attached these isnads at its beginning. By them he intends that what he narrated of tafsir in this book does not go outside these isnads. I can hardly conceive that he narrated every letter of these tafsirs from all of them. Rather it is a book composed in tafsir, with reference to narration from these people in general, not in detail.

What caused people to fall into this confusion is the dispersal of these tafsirs in their places, as in the practice of al-Tabari before us, and as in the practice of Ibn Abi Hatim as narrated by al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar, and as in the practice of al-Hakim in the Mustadrak. I almost affirm that this dispersal is an error on their part, because it gives the reader the impression that every letter of these tafsirs is narrated with all these isnads, since they set them out in full at each isnad, while al-Hakim selects from them a single isnad which he mentions with each tafsir he wishes to narrate. It may be that what al-Hakim narrated, for example, with the isnad to Ibn Mas'ud, is not what al-Suddi narrated explicitly from Ibn Mas'ud; rather it may be from what he narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, or from what people among the Companions narrated, having narrated from each of them something, so he attributed the general statement and did not attribute the details.

Al-Suddi was not unique in this, and this is not a criticism of him nor a defect in him. He intends to attribute these tafsirs to the Companions: some from Ibn 'Abbas, some from Ibn Mas'ud, and some from

And the root of their saying regarding obedience, "sami'a lahu," derives from listening (al-istima'), and it is said from it: "sami'tu laka," meaning "I heard your words," and "ata'tu fima qulta wa amarta" (I obeyed in what you said and commanded).

Scholars of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said similarly to what we have said regarding the meaning of His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord﴾.

Those who said so:
◆ Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened to its Lord."
◆ Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Ash'ath, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened and obeyed."
◆ Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened."
◆ al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.
◆ Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened and obeyed."
◆ Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: i.e., it listened and obeyed.
◆ I was told from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened and obeyed."

* *

As for His words: ﴿and is bound to﴾
It means: God made the listening incumbent upon it by the splitting and by its arriving at obedience to Him in that.
Scholars of interpretation said similarly to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said so:
◆ Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿and is bound to﴾: he said: "It was made bound to obey its Lord."
◆ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Jarir narrated to us, from Ash'ath ibn Ishaq, from Ja'far, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿and is bound to﴾: "and it is right for it."

* *

As for His words: ﴿And when the earth is stretched out﴾
God, exalted is He, says: and when the earth is spread out and increased in its extent.
Like what was reported:
◆ Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, from 'Ali ibn Husayn, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, God will stretch out the earth until there is for no human being except the place of his two feet. I will be the first to be called, and Gabriel will be at the right of the Most Merciful, and by God he had not seen him before. I will say: 'O Lord, this one informed me that You sent him to me,' and He will say: 'He has spoken truly.' Then I will intercede, and I will say: 'O Lord, Your servants have worshipped You at the ends of the earth.' He said: 'And that is the Praised Station (al-maqam al-mahmud).'"
◆ Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿is stretched out﴾: "On the Day of Resurrection."

* *

As for His words: ﴿And it casts forth what is within it and empties itself﴾
God, may His praise be exalted, says: the earth cast out what was in its belly of the dead onto its surface, and emptied itself of them before God.
Scholars of interpretation said similarly to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said so:
◆ Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿And it casts forth what is within it and empties itself﴾: he said: "It brought out what was in it of the dead."
◆ Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿And it casts forth what is within it and empties itself﴾: he said: "It brought out its burdens and what was in it."

* *

As for His words: ﴿And hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾
It means: the earth listened, in its casting forth what was in its belly of the dead onto its surface alive, to the command of its Lord, and obeyed. ﴿And is bound to﴾: it means that God made it bound to listen to His command in that, and to arrive at obedience to Him.

The scholars of Arabic grammar differed over where the answer (jawab) to His words ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ and His words ﴿And when the earth is stretched out﴾ lies.

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ carries the meaning of His words ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾, so that the sense is: when the sky is split open (you will meet your Lord), by way of anticipation and postponement (al-taqdim wa al-ta'khir).

And some of the grammarians of Kufa said: Some of the exegetes said: the answer to ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ is His words ﴿and it hearkens to its Lord﴾. He said: We hold that this is an opinion that the exegete arrived at, and he compared it to the words of God Most High: ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾. For we have not heard an answer beginning with the letter waw (و) after an initial idha (إذا) that is not preceded by speech, nor with idha when it begins a clause. He said: The Arabs only use waw in the answer in phrases such as "حتى إذا كان" (until when it was) and "فلما أن كان" (so when it was), and they do not go beyond that. He said: The answer in ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ and in ﴿When the earth is stretched out﴾ is as if omitted, because the meaning is known and its meaning has been repeated in the Qur'an, so it is understood. And if you wish, its answer may be: ﴿O mankind﴾, like the saying of a speaker: "When such-and-such occurs, then, O people, you will see what you have done of good or evil," making ﴿O mankind﴾ the answer, with a fa' (ف) implied in it. The answer to ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ has also been explained as what a person encounters of reward and punishment, as if the meaning is: you will see the reward and the punishment when the sky is split open.

The correct view on this matter, in our opinion, is that its answer is omitted, left out because the addressees know its meaning. The sense of the speech is: ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ a person will see what he has sent forward of good or evil. This is made clear by His words ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾ and the verses that follow.

For this reason al-Bukhari did not heed this statement of al-Sha'bi and did not narrate it; rather, he narrated in al-Kabir from Musaddad from Yahya who said: "I heard Ibn Abi Khalid say: al-Suddi is more knowledgeable of the Qur'an than al-Sha'bi." He narrated in his two histories from Ibn al-Madini from Yahya, namely al-Qattan, who said: "I have never seen anyone mention al-Suddi except with good, and no one abandoned him." In al-Tahdhib: "al-'Ijli said: trustworthy, a scholar of tafsir, and a transmitter of it." We have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad 807. al-Suddi died in the year 127.

And "al-Suddi": with a damma on the sin and a shadda on the dal (unpointed letters), a nisba to "al-Sudda," which is the door, because he used to sit at the sudda of the mosque in Kufa and sell head-coverings there.

Abu Malik: he is al-Ghifari, whose name is Ghazwan. He is a trustworthy Kufan Tabi'i. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 4/1/108, Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat 6: 206, and Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 3/2/55, and Yahya ibn Ma'in's authentication of him was narrated.

Abu Salih: he is the client of Umm Hani bint Abi Talib, whose name is Badham, and it is said Badhan. He is a trustworthy Tabi'i. We have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad 2030. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 1/2/144, and narrated from Muhammad ibn Bashshar who said: "Ibn Mahdi abandoned the hadith of Abu Salih." Likewise Ibn Abi Hatim narrated in his biography in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/431–432 from Ahmad ibn Hanbal from Ibn Mahdi. But he also narrated from Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan who said: "I have not seen anyone of our companions abandon Abu Salih, the client of Umm Hani, and I have not heard anyone say anything about him; Shu'ba, Za'ida, and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman did not abandon him." He also narrated from Yahya ibn Ma'in who said: "Abu Salih, client of Umm Hani, is not objectionable; but when al-Kalbi narrates from him, he is worth nothing, and when anyone other than al-Kalbi narrates from him, there is nothing objectionable in him, because al-Kalbi narrates it sometimes from his own opinion, sometimes from Abu Salih, and sometimes from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas." He means by this that the criticism concerning what he narrates is in the narration of al-Kalbi, as is evident.

This concludes the first part of this isnad, for in reality it is two or three isnads. The first is this one connected to Ibn 'Abbas.

The second part, or second isnad: "and from Murra al-Hamdani from Ibn Mas'ud." The one who narrates from Murra al-Hamdani is al-Suddi himself.

Murra: he is Ibn Sharahil al-Hamdani al-Kufi, a trustworthy Tabi'i, one of the senior Tabi'un, about whom there is no disagreement among them.

The third part, or third isnad: "and from people among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ."

This too is from al-Suddi's own transmission from some Companions.

So al-Suddi narrates these interpretations of Qur'anic verses: from two Tabi'un from Ibn 'Abbas, from one Tabi'i from Ibn Mas'ud, and from his own transmission from some Companions.

The early imams of the scholars have spoken about this tafsir with these isnads, in a way that may give the impression that it was composed by someone other than al-Suddi among those who narrated from him. However, I have since become certain that it is a book which al-Suddi composed.

Among that is the statement of Ibn Sa'd in the biography of "'Amr ibn Hammad al-Qannad" 6: 285: "companion of the tafsir of Asbat ibn Nasr from al-Suddi." He said in the biography of "Asbat ibn Nasr" 6: 261: "He was a transmitter of al-Suddi, from whom he narrated the tafsir." He said before that in the biography of "al-Suddi" 6: 225: "Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Suddi, the author of the tafsir." He said before that also, in the biography of "Abu Malik al-Ghifari" 6: 206: "Abu Malik al-Ghifari, author of the tafsir, and he had little hadith."

But what indicates that it is a book composed by al-Suddi, in which he gathered the tafsir through these three routes, is the statement of Ahmad ibn Hanbal in al-Tahdhib 1: 314, in the biography of al-Suddi: "He is good in hadith, except that this tafsir which he brings has been given an isnad and he has taxed himself for it." And the statement of al-Hafiz in al-Tahdhib also 1: 315: "al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim and others have transmitted the tafsir of al-Suddi in their tafsirs, dispersed among the surahs, through the route of Asbat ibn Nasr from him."

And the statement of al-Suyuti in al-Itqan 2: 224, as quoted from al-Khalil in al-Irshad: "The tafsir of Isma'il al-Suddi, he narrates it with isnads to Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. The imams narrated from al-Suddi, such as al-Thawri and Shu'ba. But the tafsir which he compiled was narrated by Asbat ibn Nasr, and the scholars did not agree on Asbat. Nevertheless, the most excellent of tafsirs is the tafsir of al-Suddi." Then al-Suyuti said: "The tafsir of al-Suddi, which he referred to, Ibn Jarir narrates much of it through the route of al-Suddi from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murra from Ibn Mas'ud, and [from] people among the Companions. Thus. Ibn Abi Hatim did not narrate anything of it, because he committed himself to bringing out only the most authentic that was transmitted. Al-Hakim brings out some of it in his Mustadrak and authenticates it, but only through the route of Murra from Ibn Mas'ud and the people, alone, without the first route. Ibn Kathir said: this isnad through which al-Suddi narrates things contains strangeness."

The first thing we point out in these statements: the contradiction between the two statements of al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar and al-Suyuti, regarding whether Ibn Abi Hatim brought out the tafsir of al-Suddi dispersed in his tafsir, as al-Tabari did, according to al-Hafiz's transmission, and that he turned away from it, according to al-Suyuti's transmission. I cannot assert anything definite about this, since I have not seen the tafsir of Ibn Abi Hatim. But I lean toward preferring Ibn Hajar's transmission, as he is more careful and precise in transmission than al-Suyuti.

Then al-Suyuti was right about what he transmitted from al-Hakim. For he narrates some of this tafsir in the Mustadrak, with its isnad, to Ahmad ibn Nasr: "Ahmad ibn 'Amr ibn Talha al-Qannad narrated to us, Asbat ibn Nasr narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Suddi, from Murra al-Hamdani, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and from some people among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ." Then he authenticates it on the condition of Muslim, and al-Dhahabi agrees with him in his summary. Such as in the Mustadrak 2: 258, 260, 273, 321.

Al-Hakim is correct in this, for Muslim narrated from all the narrators of this isnad, from 'Amr ibn Hammad ibn Talha al-Qannad to Murra al-Hamdani. He did not narrate from Abu Salih Badham or from Abu Malik al-Ghifari, in the first part of the isnad through which al-Suddi narrated his tafsirs.

As for the words of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal about al-Suddi, "except that this tafsir which he brings has been given an isnad and he has taxed himself for it," he does not mean what might be understood from its apparent meaning: that he fabricated an isnad with no basis; for had that been the case, he would in his view have been a liar and a fabricator of narrations. Rather he means, in my view, and God knows best, that he gathered these tafsirs from his narration from these people: from Abu Malik and Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, from Murra from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some Companions; then he set them all out in detail, on the verses in which some interpretation was reported from this one or that one or those, and gave all of them this isnad, and took pains to present them all in a single line.

That is: he gathered the scattered tafsirs into one book, to which he attached these isnads at its beginning. By them he intends that what he narrated of tafsir in this book does not go outside these isnads. I can hardly conceive that he narrated every letter of these tafsirs from all of them. Rather it is a book composed in tafsir, with reference to narration from these people in general, not in detail.

What caused people to fall into this confusion is the dispersal of these tafsirs in their places, as in the practice of al-Tabari before us, and as in the practice of Ibn Abi Hatim as narrated by al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar, and as in the practice of al-Hakim in the Mustadrak. I almost affirm that this dispersal is an error on their part, because it gives the reader the impression that every letter of these tafsirs is narrated with all these isnads, since they set them out in full at each isnad, while al-Hakim selects from them a single isnad which he mentions with each tafsir he wishes to narrate. It may be that what al-Hakim narrated, for example, with the isnad to Ibn Mas'ud, is not what al-Suddi narrated explicitly from Ibn Mas'ud; rather it may be from what he narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, or from what people among the Companions narrated, having narrated from each of them something, so he attributed the general statement and did not attribute the details.

Al-Suddi was not unique in this, and this is not a criticism of him nor a defect in him. He intends to attribute these tafsirs to the Companions: some from Ibn 'Abbas, some from Ibn Mas'ud, and some from

And the root of their saying regarding obedience, "sami'a lahu," derives from listening (al-istima'), and it is said from it: "sami'tu laka," meaning "I heard your words," and "ata'tu fima qulta wa amarta" (I obeyed in what you said and commanded).

Scholars of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said similarly to what we have said regarding the meaning of His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord﴾.

Those who said so:
◆ Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened to its Lord."
◆ Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Ash'ath, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened and obeyed."
◆ Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened."
◆ al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.
◆ Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened and obeyed."
◆ Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: i.e., it listened and obeyed.
◆ I was told from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened and obeyed."

* *

As for His words: ﴿and is bound to﴾
It means: God made the listening incumbent upon it by the splitting and by its arriving at obedience to Him in that.
Scholars of interpretation said similarly to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said so:
◆ Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿and is bound to﴾: he said: "It was made bound to obey its Lord."
◆ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Jarir narrated to us, from Ash'ath ibn Ishaq, from Ja'far, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿and is bound to﴾: "and it is right for it."

* *

As for His words: ﴿And when the earth is stretched out﴾
God, exalted is He, says: and when the earth is spread out and increased in its extent.
Like what was reported:
◆ Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, from 'Ali ibn Husayn, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, God will stretch out the earth until there is for no human being except the place of his two feet. I will be the first to be called, and Gabriel will be at the right of the Most Merciful, and by God he had not seen him before. I will say: 'O Lord, this one informed me that You sent him to me,' and He will say: 'He has spoken truly.' Then I will intercede, and I will say: 'O Lord, Your servants have worshipped You at the ends of the earth.' He said: 'And that is the Praised Station (al-maqam al-mahmud).'"
◆ Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿is stretched out﴾: "On the Day of Resurrection."

* *

As for His words: ﴿And it casts forth what is within it and empties itself﴾
God, may His praise be exalted, says: the earth cast out what was in its belly of the dead onto its surface, and emptied itself of them before God.
Scholars of interpretation said similarly to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said so:
◆ Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿And it casts forth what is within it and empties itself﴾: he said: "It brought out what was in it of the dead."
◆ Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿And it casts forth what is within it and empties itself﴾: he said: "It brought out its burdens and what was in it."

* *

As for His words: ﴿And hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾
It means: the earth listened, in its casting forth what was in its belly of the dead onto its surface alive, to the command of its Lord, and obeyed. ﴿And is bound to﴾: it means that God made it bound to listen to His command in that, and to arrive at obedience to Him.

The scholars of Arabic grammar differed over where the answer (jawab) to His words ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ and His words ﴿And when the earth is stretched out﴾ lies.

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ carries the meaning of His words ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾, so that the sense is: when the sky is split open (you will meet your Lord), by way of anticipation and postponement (al-taqdim wa al-ta'khir).

And some of the grammarians of Kufa said: Some of the exegetes said: the answer to ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ is His words ﴿and it hearkens to its Lord﴾. He said: We hold that this is an opinion that the exegete arrived at, and he compared it to the words of God Most High: ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾. For we have not heard an answer beginning with the letter waw (و) after an initial idha (إذا) that is not preceded by speech, nor with idha when it begins a clause. He said: The Arabs only use waw in the answer in phrases such as "حتى إذا كان" (until when it was) and "فلما أن كان" (so when it was), and they do not go beyond that. He said: The answer in ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ and in ﴿When the earth is stretched out﴾ is as if omitted, because the meaning is known and its meaning has been repeated in the Qur'an, so it is understood. And if you wish, its answer may be: ﴿O mankind﴾, like the saying of a speaker: "When such-and-such occurs, then, O people, you will see what you have done of good or evil," making ﴿O mankind﴾ the answer, with a fa' (ف) implied in it. The answer to ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ has also been explained as what a person encounters of reward and punishment, as if the meaning is: you will see the reward and the punishment when the sky is split open.

The correct view on this matter, in our opinion, is that its answer is omitted, left out because the addressees know its meaning. The sense of the speech is: ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ a person will see what he has sent forward of good or evil. This is made clear by His words ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾ and the verses that follow.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 84, verse 1–5 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿When the sky is split asunder (1) and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to (2). And when the earth is stretched out (3) and casts forth what is within it and empties itself (4) and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to (5).﴾

God, exalted is He, says: when the sky is split and torn apart, so that it becomes gates.

* *

As for His words, ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾:
It means: the heavens, in their splitting and cleaving, listen to their Lord and obey Him in His command to them. The Arabs say: "adhina lak fi hadha al-amr adhanan," meaning: "he listened to you," and from this is the report transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ: "God has not listened to anything as He listens to a Prophet who chants the Qur'an" (ma adhina Allahu li-shay'in ka-adhanihi li-nabiyyin yataghanna bil-Qur'an), meaning: God has not listened to anything as He listens to a Prophet who chants the Qur'an. And from it is the verse of the poet:
Deaf when they hear good spoken of me, ...
but when evil is mentioned of me in their presence, they listen (adhinu).[[The report 168 – this isnad is among the most frequently recurring isnads in the tafsir of al-Tabari, if not the most frequent; it is hardly possible for the interpretation of any verse to be free of a narration with this isnad. Al-Tabari himself expressed doubt about it in (p. 121 Bulaq, line 28 and following), when he mentioned the report from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas with this isnad, saying: "If that is sound – and I do not know it to be sound, since its isnad is doubtful to me..." He did not explain the cause of his doubt regarding its isnad, and despite his doubt he narrated through it extensively, yet he never made it a proof.

However, I see it as an isnad requiring careful investigation. The scholars of hadith have spoken about it and about some of its narrators. I have traced what they said and what its investigation calls for, as far as I could, and an opinion has appeared to me which I hope is correct, God willing. My success is only through God:

As for Al-Tabari's teacher, "Musa ibn Harun al-Hamdani": I have not found a biography of him, nor any mention of him in any of the references available to me, except what al-Tabari also narrates from him in his History, more than fifty times in its first and second volumes. There is no need for us to examine his biography in terms of jarh wa ta'dil (criticism and validation), for this tafsir which he narrates from 'Amr ibn Hammad is known among the people of hadith scholarship, and it is merely the transmission of a book, not the transmission of a particular hadith.

"And 'Amr ibn Hammad": he is 'Amr ibn Hammad ibn Talha al-Qannad, and he is sometimes attributed to his grandfather, so it is said 'Amr ibn Talha. He is trustworthy (thiqa). Muslim narrated from him in his Sahih. Ibn Sa'd included his biography in al-Tabaqat 6: 285 and said: "He was trustworthy, God willing." He died in the year 222. Ibn Abi Hatim included his biography in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 3/1/228, and narrated from his father and from Yahya ibn Ma'in that they both said of him: "Sadduq" (truthful).

Asbat ibn Nasr al-Hamdani: he is disputed. Ahmad weakened him, and Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat: 410. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 1/2/53 and did not mention any criticism of him. Ibn Abi Hatim included his biography in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/332 and narrated from Yahya ibn Ma'in who said: "Asbat ibn Nasr is trustworthy." We have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad, in hadith 1286.

Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Karima al-Suddi: he is al-Suddi al-Kabir, a Qurashi by clientage (mawla), client of Zaynab bint Qays ibn Makhrama, from the Banu 'Abd Manaf, as al-Bukhari stated in his two histories: al-Saghir: 141–142, and al-Kabir 1/1/361. He was a Tabi'i. He heard Anas, as al-Bukhari also stated, and narrated from other Companions and from many Tabi'un. He is trustworthy. Muslim narrated from him in his Sahih. Ahmad ibn Hanbal authenticated him, as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/184, and he also narrated from Ahmad who said: "Yahya ibn Ma'in once said to me in the presence of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi: al-Suddi is weak. 'Abd al-Rahman became angry and disliked what he said." In al-Mizan and al-Tahdhib it is said that al-Sha'bi was told: "al-Suddi has been given a portion of knowledge of the Qur'an," and he said: "He has been given a portion of ignorance of the Qur'an!" In my view this statement of al-Sha'bi may be the basis for the words of everyone who spoke about al-Suddi unjustly. For this reason al-Bukhari did not heed this statement of al-Sha'bi and did not narrate it; rather, he narrated in al-Kabir from Musaddad from Yahya who said: "I heard Ibn Abi Khalid say: al-Suddi is more knowledgeable of the Qur'an than al-Sha'bi." He narrated in his two histories from Ibn al-Madini from Yahya, namely al-Qattan, who said: "I have never seen anyone mention al-Suddi except with good, and no one abandoned him." In al-Tahdhib: "al-'Ijli said: trustworthy, a scholar of tafsir, and a transmitter of it." We have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad 807. al-Suddi died in the year 127.

And "al-Suddi": with a damma on the sin and a shadda on the dal (unpointed letters), a nisba to "al-Sudda," which is the door, because he used to sit at the sudda of the mosque in Kufa and sell head-coverings there.

Abu Malik: he is al-Ghifari, whose name is Ghazwan. He is a trustworthy Kufan Tabi'i. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 4/1/108, Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat 6: 206, and Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 3/2/55, and Yahya ibn Ma'in's authentication of him was narrated.

Abu Salih: he is the client of Umm Hani bint Abi Talib, whose name is Badham, and it is said Badhan. He is a trustworthy Tabi'i. We have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad 2030. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 1/2/144, and narrated from Muhammad ibn Bashshar who said: "Ibn Mahdi abandoned the hadith of Abu Salih." Likewise Ibn Abi Hatim narrated in his biography in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/431–432 from Ahmad ibn Hanbal from Ibn Mahdi. But he also narrated from Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan who said: "I have not seen anyone of our companions abandon Abu Salih, the client of Umm Hani, and I have not heard anyone say anything about him; Shu'ba, Za'ida, and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman did not abandon him." He also narrated from Yahya ibn Ma'in who said: "Abu Salih, client of Umm Hani, is not objectionable; but when al-Kalbi narrates from him, he is worth nothing, and when anyone other than al-Kalbi narrates from him, there is nothing objectionable in him, because al-Kalbi narrates it sometimes from his own opinion, sometimes from Abu Salih, and sometimes from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas." He means by this that the criticism concerning what he narrates is in the narration of al-Kalbi, as is evident.

This concludes the first part of this isnad, for in reality it is two or three isnads. The first is this one connected to Ibn 'Abbas.

The second part, or second isnad: "and from Murra al-Hamdani from Ibn Mas'ud." The one who narrates from Murra al-Hamdani is al-Suddi himself.

Murra: he is Ibn Sharahil al-Hamdani al-Kufi, a trustworthy Tabi'i, one of the senior Tabi'un, about whom there is no disagreement among them.

The third part, or third isnad: "and from people among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ."

This too is from al-Suddi's own transmission from some Companions.

So al-Suddi narrates these interpretations of Qur'anic verses: from two Tabi'un from Ibn 'Abbas, from one Tabi'i from Ibn Mas'ud, and from his own transmission from some Companions.

The early imams of the scholars have spoken about this tafsir with these isnads, in a way that may give the impression that it was composed by someone other than al-Suddi among those who narrated from him. However, I have since become certain that it is a book which al-Suddi composed.

Among that is the statement of Ibn Sa'd in the biography of "'Amr ibn Hammad al-Qannad" 6: 285: "companion of the tafsir of Asbat ibn Nasr from al-Suddi." He said in the biography of "Asbat ibn Nasr" 6: 261: "He was a transmitter of al-Suddi, from whom he narrated the tafsir." He said before that in the biography of "al-Suddi" 6: 225: "Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Suddi, the author of the tafsir." He said before that also, in the biography of "Abu Malik al-Ghifari" 6: 206: "Abu Malik al-Ghifari, author of the tafsir, and he had little hadith."

But what indicates that it is a book composed by al-Suddi, in which he gathered the tafsir through these three routes, is the statement of Ahmad ibn Hanbal in al-Tahdhib 1: 314, in the biography of al-Suddi: "He is good in hadith, except that this tafsir which he brings has been given an isnad and he has taxed himself for it." And the statement of al-Hafiz in al-Tahdhib also 1: 315: "al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim and others have transmitted the tafsir of al-Suddi in their tafsirs, dispersed among the surahs, through the route of Asbat ibn Nasr from him."

And the statement of al-Suyuti in al-Itqan 2: 224, as quoted from al-Khalil in al-Irshad: "The tafsir of Isma'il al-Suddi, he narrates it with isnads to Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. The imams narrated from al-Suddi, such as al-Thawri and Shu'ba. But the tafsir which he compiled was narrated by Asbat ibn Nasr, and the scholars did not agree on Asbat. Nevertheless, the most excellent of tafsirs is the tafsir of al-Suddi." Then al-Suyuti said: "The tafsir of al-Suddi, which he referred to, Ibn Jarir narrates much of it through the route of al-Suddi from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murra from Ibn Mas'ud, and [from] people among the Companions. Thus. Ibn Abi Hatim did not narrate anything of it, because he committed himself to bringing out only the most authentic that was transmitted. Al-Hakim brings out some of it in his Mustadrak and authenticates it, but only through the route of Murra from Ibn Mas'ud and the people, alone, without the first route. Ibn Kathir said: this isnad through which al-Suddi narrates things contains strangeness."

The first thing we point out in these statements: the contradiction between the two statements of al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar and al-Suyuti, regarding whether Ibn Abi Hatim brought out the tafsir of al-Suddi dispersed in his tafsir, as al-Tabari did, according to al-Hafiz's transmission, and that he turned away from it, according to al-Suyuti's transmission. I cannot assert anything definite about this, since I have not seen the tafsir of Ibn Abi Hatim. But I lean toward preferring Ibn Hajar's transmission, as he is more careful and precise in transmission than al-Suyuti.

Then al-Suyuti was right about what he transmitted from al-Hakim. For he narrates some of this tafsir in the Mustadrak, with its isnad, to Ahmad ibn Nasr: "Ahmad ibn 'Amr ibn Talha al-Qannad narrated to us, Asbat ibn Nasr narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Suddi, from Murra al-Hamdani, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and from some people among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ." Then he authenticates it on the condition of Muslim, and al-Dhahabi agrees with him in his summary. Such as in the Mustadrak 2: 258, 260, 273, 321.

Al-Hakim is correct in this, for Muslim narrated from all the narrators of this isnad, from 'Amr ibn Hammad ibn Talha al-Qannad to Murra al-Hamdani. He did not narrate from Abu Salih Badham or from Abu Malik al-Ghifari, in the first part of the isnad through which al-Suddi narrated his tafsirs.

As for the words of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal about al-Suddi, "except that this tafsir which he brings has been given an isnad and he has taxed himself for it," he does not mean what might be understood from its apparent meaning: that he fabricated an isnad with no basis; for had that been the case, he would in his view have been a liar and a fabricator of narrations. Rather he means, in my view, and God knows best, that he gathered these tafsirs from his narration from these people: from Abu Malik and Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, from Murra from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some Companions; then he set them all out in detail, on the verses in which some interpretation was reported from this one or that one or those, and gave all of them this isnad, and took pains to present them all in a single line.

That is: he gathered the scattered tafsirs into one book, to which he attached these isnads at its beginning. By them he intends that what he narrated of tafsir in this book does not go outside these isnads. I can hardly conceive that he narrated every letter of these tafsirs from all of them. Rather it is a book composed in tafsir, with reference to narration from these people in general, not in detail.

What caused people to fall into this confusion is the dispersal of these tafsirs in their places, as in the practice of al-Tabari before us, and as in the practice of Ibn Abi Hatim as narrated by al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar, and as in the practice of al-Hakim in the Mustadrak. I almost affirm that this dispersal is an error on their part, because it gives the reader the impression that every letter of these tafsirs is narrated with all these isnads, since they set them out in full at each isnad, while al-Hakim selects from them a single isnad which he mentions with each tafsir he wishes to narrate. It may be that what al-Hakim narrated, for example, with the isnad to Ibn Mas'ud, is not what al-Suddi narrated explicitly from Ibn Mas'ud; rather it may be from what he narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, or from what people among the Companions narrated, having narrated from each of them something, so he attributed the general statement and did not attribute the details.

Al-Suddi was not unique in this, and this is not a criticism of him nor a defect in him. He intends to attribute these tafsirs to the Companions: some from Ibn 'Abbas, some from Ibn Mas'ud, and some from

And the root of their saying regarding obedience, "sami'a lahu," derives from listening (al-istima'), and it is said from it: "sami'tu laka," meaning "I heard your words," and "ata'tu fima qulta wa amarta" (I obeyed in what you said and commanded).

Scholars of interpretation (ahl al-ta'wil) said similarly to what we have said regarding the meaning of His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord﴾.

Those who said so:
◆ Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened to its Lord."
◆ Abu Kurayb narrated to us, he said: Ibn Yaman narrated to us, from Ash'ath, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened and obeyed."
◆ Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened."
◆ al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.
◆ Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened and obeyed."
◆ Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: i.e., it listened and obeyed.
◆ I was told from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened and obeyed."

As for His words: ﴿and is bound to﴾
It means: God made the listening incumbent upon it by the splitting and by its arriving at obedience to Him in that.
Scholars of interpretation said similarly to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said so:
◆ Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿and is bound to﴾: he said: "It was made bound to obey its Lord."
◆ Ibn Humayd narrated to us, he said: Jarir narrated to us, from Ash'ath ibn Ishaq, from Ja'far, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: ﴿and is bound to﴾: "and it is right for it."

* *

As for His words: ﴿And when the earth is stretched out﴾
God, exalted is He, says: and when the earth is spread out and increased in its extent.
Like what was reported:
◆ Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from al-Zuhri, from 'Ali ibn Husayn, that the Prophet ﷺ said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, God will stretch out the earth until there is for no human being except the place of his two feet. I will be the first to be called, and Gabriel will be at the right of the Most Merciful, and by God he had not seen him before. I will say: 'O Lord, this one informed me that You sent him to me,' and He will say: 'He has spoken truly.' Then I will intercede, and I will say: 'O Lord, Your servants have worshipped You at the ends of the earth.' He said: 'And that is the Praised Station (al-maqam al-mahmud).'"
◆ Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿is stretched out﴾: "On the Day of Resurrection."

* *

As for His words: ﴿And it casts forth what is within it and empties itself﴾
God, may His praise be exalted, says: the earth cast out what was in its belly of the dead onto its surface, and emptied itself of them before God.
Scholars of interpretation said similarly to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said so:
◆ Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿And it casts forth what is within it and empties itself﴾: he said: "It brought out what was in it of the dead."
◆ Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿And it casts forth what is within it and empties itself﴾: he said: "It brought out its burdens and what was in it."

* *

As for His words: ﴿And hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾
It means: the earth listened, in its casting forth what was in its belly of the dead onto its surface alive, to the command of its Lord, and obeyed. ﴿And is bound to﴾: it means that God made it bound to listen to His command in that, and to arrive at obedience to Him.

The scholars of Arabic grammar differed over where the answer (jawab) to His words ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ and His words ﴿And when the earth is stretched out﴾ lies.

Some of the grammarians of Basra said: ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ carries the meaning of His words ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾, so that the sense is: when the sky is split open (you will meet your Lord), by way of anticipation and postponement (al-taqdim wa al-ta'khir).

And some of the grammarians of Kufa said: Some of the exegetes said: the answer to ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ is His words ﴿and it hearkens to its Lord﴾. He said: We hold that this is an opinion that the exegete arrived at, and he compared it to the words of God Most High: ﴿until, when they reach it and its gates are opened﴾. For we have not heard an answer beginning with the letter waw (و) after an initial idha (إذا) that is not preceded by speech, nor with idha when it begins a clause. He said: The Arabs only use waw in the answer in phrases such as "حتى إذا كان" (until when it was) and "فلما أن كان" (so when it was), and they do not go beyond that. He said: The answer in ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ and in ﴿When the earth is stretched out﴾ is as if omitted, because the meaning is known and its meaning has been repeated in the Qur'an, so it is understood. And if you wish, its answer may be: ﴿O mankind﴾, like the saying of a speaker: "When such-and-such occurs, then, O people, you will see what you have done of good or evil," making ﴿O mankind﴾ the answer, with a fa' (ف) implied in it. The answer to ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ has also been explained as what a person encounters of reward and punishment, as if the meaning is: you will see the reward and the punishment when the sky is split open.

The correct view on this matter, in our opinion, is that its answer is omitted, left out because the addressees know its meaning. The sense of the speech is: ﴿When the sky is split open﴾ a person will see what he has sent forward of good or evil. This is made clear by His words ﴿O mankind, indeed you are laboring toward your Lord with labor, and you will meet Him﴾ and the verses that follow.

Commentary of al-Tabari (Jami al-Bayan) on surah 84, verse 1–5 (part 1 of 2):

The interpretation of the words of God, exalted is He: ﴿When the sky is split asunder (1) and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to (2). And when the earth is stretched out (3) and casts forth what is within it and empties itself (4) and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to (5).﴾

God, exalted is He, says: when the sky is split and torn apart, so that it becomes gates.

* *

As for His words, ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾:
It means: the heavens, in their splitting and cleaving, listen to their Lord and obey Him in His command to them. The Arabs say: "adhina lak fi hadha al-amr adhanan," meaning: "he listened to you," and from this is the report transmitted from the Prophet ﷺ: "God has not listened to anything as He listens to a Prophet who chants the Qur'an" (ma adhina Allahu li-shay'in ka-adhanihi li-nabiyyin yataghanna bil-Qur'an), meaning: God has not listened to anything as He listens to a Prophet who chants the Qur'an. And from it is the verse of the poet:
Deaf when they hear good spoken of me, ...
but when evil is mentioned of me in their presence, they listen (adhinu).[[The report 168 – this isnad is among the most frequently recurring isnads in the tafsir of al-Tabari, if not the most frequent; it is hardly possible for the interpretation of any verse to be free of a narration with this isnad. Al-Tabari himself expressed doubt about it in (p. 121 Bulaq, line 28 and following), when he mentioned the report from Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas with this isnad, saying: "If that is sound – and I do not know it to be sound, since its isnad is doubtful to me..." He did not explain the cause of his doubt regarding its isnad, and despite his doubt he narrated through it extensively, yet he never made it a proof.

However, I see it as an isnad requiring careful investigation. The scholars of hadith have spoken about it and about some of its narrators. I have traced what they said and what its investigation calls for, as far as I could, and an opinion has appeared to me which I hope is correct, God willing. My success is only through God:

As for Al-Tabari's teacher, "Musa ibn Harun al-Hamdani": I have not found a biography of him, nor any mention of him in any of the references available to me, except what al-Tabari also narrates from him in his History, more than fifty times in its first and second volumes. There is no need for us to examine his biography in terms of jarh wa ta'dil (criticism and validation), for this tafsir which he narrates from 'Amr ibn Hammad is known among the people of hadith scholarship, and it is merely the transmission of a book, not the transmission of a particular hadith.

"And 'Amr ibn Hammad": he is 'Amr ibn Hammad ibn Talha al-Qannad, and he is sometimes attributed to his grandfather, so it is said 'Amr ibn Talha. He is trustworthy (thiqa). Muslim narrated from him in his Sahih. Ibn Sa'd included his biography in al-Tabaqat 6: 285 and said: "He was trustworthy, God willing." He died in the year 222. Ibn Abi Hatim included his biography in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 3/1/228, and narrated from his father and from Yahya ibn Ma'in that they both said of him: "Sadduq" (truthful).

Asbat ibn Nasr al-Hamdani: he is disputed. Ahmad weakened him, and Ibn Hibban mentioned him in al-Thiqat: 410. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 1/2/53 and did not mention any criticism of him. Ibn Abi Hatim included his biography in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/332 and narrated from Yahya ibn Ma'in who said: "Asbat ibn Nasr is trustworthy." We have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad, in hadith 1286.

Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Abi Karima al-Suddi: he is al-Suddi al-Kabir, a Qurashi by clientage (mawla), client of Zaynab bint Qays ibn Makhrama, from the Banu 'Abd Manaf, as al-Bukhari stated in his two histories: al-Saghir: 141–142, and al-Kabir 1/1/361. He was a Tabi'i. He heard Anas, as al-Bukhari also stated, and narrated from other Companions and from many Tabi'un. He is trustworthy. Muslim narrated from him in his Sahih. Ahmad ibn Hanbal authenticated him, as Ibn Abi Hatim narrated in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/184, and he also narrated from Ahmad who said: "Yahya ibn Ma'in once said to me in the presence of 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Mahdi: al-Suddi is weak. 'Abd al-Rahman became angry and disliked what he said." In al-Mizan and al-Tahdhib it is said that al-Sha'bi was told: "al-Suddi has been given a portion of knowledge of the Qur'an," and he said: "He has been given a portion of ignorance of the Qur'an!" In my view this statement of al-Sha'bi may be the basis for the words of everyone who spoke about al-Suddi unjustly. For this reason al-Bukhari did not heed this statement of al-Sha'bi and did not narrate it; rather, he narrated in al-Kabir from Musaddad from Yahya who said: "I heard Ibn Abi Khalid say: al-Suddi is more knowledgeable of the Qur'an than al-Sha'bi." He narrated in his two histories from Ibn al-Madini from Yahya, namely al-Qattan, who said: "I have never seen anyone mention al-Suddi except with good, and no one abandoned him." In al-Tahdhib: "al-'Ijli said: trustworthy, a scholar of tafsir, and a transmitter of it." We have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad 807. al-Suddi died in the year 127.

And "al-Suddi": with a damma on the sin and a shadda on the dal (unpointed letters), a nisba to "al-Sudda," which is the door, because he used to sit at the sudda of the mosque in Kufa and sell head-coverings there.

Abu Malik: he is al-Ghifari, whose name is Ghazwan. He is a trustworthy Kufan Tabi'i. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 4/1/108, Ibn Sa'd in al-Tabaqat 6: 206, and Ibn Abi Hatim in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 3/2/55, and Yahya ibn Ma'in's authentication of him was narrated.

Abu Salih: he is the client of Umm Hani bint Abi Talib, whose name is Badham, and it is said Badhan. He is a trustworthy Tabi'i. We have preferred his authentication in our commentary on the Musnad 2030. Al-Bukhari included his biography in al-Kabir 1/2/144, and narrated from Muhammad ibn Bashshar who said: "Ibn Mahdi abandoned the hadith of Abu Salih." Likewise Ibn Abi Hatim narrated in his biography in al-Jarh wa al-Ta'dil 1/1/431–432 from Ahmad ibn Hanbal from Ibn Mahdi. But he also narrated from Yahya ibn Sa'id al-Qattan who said: "I have not seen anyone of our companions abandon Abu Salih, the client of Umm Hani, and I have not heard anyone say anything about him; Shu'ba, Za'ida, and 'Abd Allah ibn 'Uthman did not abandon him." He also narrated from Yahya ibn Ma'in who said: "Abu Salih, client of Umm Hani, is not objectionable; but when al-Kalbi narrates from him, he is worth nothing, and when anyone other than al-Kalbi narrates from him, there is nothing objectionable in him, because al-Kalbi narrates it sometimes from his own opinion, sometimes from Abu Salih, and sometimes from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas." He means by this that the criticism concerning what he narrates is in the narration of al-Kalbi, as is evident.

This concludes the first part of this isnad, for in reality it is two or three isnads. The first is this one connected to Ibn 'Abbas.

The second part, or second isnad: "and from Murra al-Hamdani from Ibn Mas'ud." The one who narrates from Murra al-Hamdani is al-Suddi himself.

Murra: he is Ibn Sharahil al-Hamdani al-Kufi, a trustworthy Tabi'i, one of the senior Tabi'un, about whom there is no disagreement among them.

The third part, or third isnad: "and from people among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ."

This too is from al-Suddi's own transmission from some Companions.

So al-Suddi narrates these interpretations of Qur'anic verses: from two Tabi'un from Ibn 'Abbas, from one Tabi'i from Ibn Mas'ud, and from his own transmission from some Companions.

The early imams of the scholars have spoken about this tafsir with these isnads, in a way that may give the impression that it was composed by someone other than al-Suddi among those who narrated from him. However, I have since become certain that it is a book which al-Suddi composed.

Among that is the statement of Ibn Sa'd in the biography of "'Amr ibn Hammad al-Qannad" 6: 285: "companion of the tafsir of Asbat ibn Nasr from al-Suddi." He said in the biography of "Asbat ibn Nasr" 6: 261: "He was a transmitter of al-Suddi, from whom he narrated the tafsir." He said before that in the biography of "al-Suddi" 6: 225: "Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Suddi, the author of the tafsir." He said before that also, in the biography of "Abu Malik al-Ghifari" 6: 206: "Abu Malik al-Ghifari, author of the tafsir, and he had little hadith."

But what indicates that it is a book composed by al-Suddi, in which he gathered the tafsir through these three routes, is the statement of Ahmad ibn Hanbal in al-Tahdhib 1: 314, in the biography of al-Suddi: "He is good in hadith, except that this tafsir which he brings has been given an isnad and he has taxed himself for it." And the statement of al-Hafiz in al-Tahdhib also 1: 315: "al-Tabari, Ibn Abi Hatim and others have transmitted the tafsir of al-Suddi in their tafsirs, dispersed among the surahs, through the route of Asbat ibn Nasr from him."

And the statement of al-Suyuti in al-Itqan 2: 224, as quoted from al-Khalil in al-Irshad: "The tafsir of Isma'il al-Suddi, he narrates it with isnads to Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn 'Abbas. The imams narrated from al-Suddi, such as al-Thawri and Shu'ba. But the tafsir which he compiled was narrated by Asbat ibn Nasr, and the scholars did not agree on Asbat. Nevertheless, the most excellent of tafsirs is the tafsir of al-Suddi." Then al-Suyuti said: "The tafsir of al-Suddi, which he referred to, Ibn Jarir narrates much of it through the route of al-Suddi from Abu Malik and from Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, and from Murra from Ibn Mas'ud, and [from] people among the Companions. Thus. Ibn Abi Hatim did not narrate anything of it, because he committed himself to bringing out only the most authentic that was transmitted. Al-Hakim brings out some of it in his Mustadrak and authenticates it, but only through the route of Murra from Ibn Mas'ud and the people, alone, without the first route. Ibn Kathir said: this isnad through which al-Suddi narrates things contains strangeness."

The first thing we point out in these statements: the contradiction between the two statements of al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar and al-Suyuti, regarding whether Ibn Abi Hatim brought out the tafsir of al-Suddi dispersed in his tafsir, as al-Tabari did, according to al-Hafiz's transmission, and that he turned away from it, according to al-Suyuti's transmission. I cannot assert anything definite about this, since I have not seen the tafsir of Ibn Abi Hatim. But I lean toward preferring Ibn Hajar's transmission, as he is more careful and precise in transmission than al-Suyuti.

Then al-Suyuti was right about what he transmitted from al-Hakim. For he narrates some of this tafsir in the Mustadrak, with its isnad, to Ahmad ibn Nasr: "Ahmad ibn 'Amr ibn Talha al-Qannad narrated to us, Asbat ibn Nasr narrated to us, from Isma'il ibn 'Abd al-Rahman al-Suddi, from Murra al-Hamdani, from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and from some people among the Companions of the Prophet ﷺ." Then he authenticates it on the condition of Muslim, and al-Dhahabi agrees with him in his summary. Such as in the Mustadrak 2: 258, 260, 273, 321.

Al-Hakim is correct in this, for Muslim narrated from all the narrators of this isnad, from 'Amr ibn Hammad ibn Talha al-Qannad to Murra al-Hamdani. He did not narrate from Abu Salih Badham or from Abu Malik al-Ghifari, in the first part of the isnad through which al-Suddi narrated his tafsirs.

As for the words of Imam Ahmad ibn Hanbal about al-Suddi, "except that this tafsir which he brings has been given an isnad and he has taxed himself for it," he does not mean what might be understood from its apparent meaning: that he fabricated an isnad with no basis; for had that been the case, he would in his view have been a liar and a fabricator of narrations. Rather he means, in my view, and God knows best, that he gathered these tafsirs from his narration from these people: from Abu Malik and Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas, from Murra from Ibn Mas'ud, and from some Companions; then he set them all out in detail, on the verses in which some interpretation was reported from this one or that one or those, and gave all of them this isnad, and took pains to present them all in a single line.

That is: he gathered the scattered tafsirs into one book, to which he attached these isnads at its beginning. By them he intends that what he narrated of tafsir in this book does not go outside these isnads. I can hardly conceive that he narrated every letter of these tafsirs from all of them. Rather it is a book composed in tafsir, with reference to narration from these people in general, not in detail.

What caused people to fall into this confusion is the dispersal of these tafsirs in their places, as in the practice of al-Tabari before us, and as in the practice of Ibn Abi Hatim as narrated by al-Hafiz Ibn Hajar, and as in the practice of al-Hakim in the Mustadrak. I almost affirm that this dispersal is an error on their part, because it gives the reader the impression that every letter of these tafsirs is narrated with all these isnads, since they set them out in full at each isnad, while al-Hakim selects from them a single isnad which he mentions with each tafsir he wishes to narrate. It may be that what al-Hakim narrated, for example, with the isnad to Ibn Mas'ud, is not what al-Suddi narrated explicitly from Ibn Mas'ud; rather it may be from what he narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, or from what people among the Companions narrated, having narrated from each of them something, so he attributed the general statement and did not attribute the details.

◆ Muhammad ibn 'Amr narrated to me, he said: Abu 'Asim narrated to us, he said: 'Isa narrated to us; and al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, all together, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened."
◆ al-Harith narrated to me, he said: al-Hasan narrated to us, he said: Warqa' narrated to us, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, similarly.
◆ Ibn 'Abd al-A'la narrated to us, he said: Ibn Thawr narrated to us, from Ma'mar, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened and obeyed."
◆ Bishr narrated to us, he said: Yazid narrated to us, he said: Sa'id narrated to us, from Qatada, regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: i.e., it listened and obeyed.
◆ I was told from al-Husayn, he said: I heard Abu Mu'adh say: 'Ubayd narrated to us, he said: I heard al-Dahhak say regarding His words: ﴿and hearkens to its Lord and is bound to﴾: he said: "It listened and obeyed."

As for His words: ﴿and is bound to﴾
It means: God made the listening incumbent upon it by the splitting and by its arriving at obedience to Him in that.
Scholars of interpretation said similarly to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said so:
◆ Muhammad ibn Sa'd narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, he said: my uncle narrated to me, he said: my father narrated to me, from his father, from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His words: ﴿and is bound to﴾: he said: "It was made bound to obey its Lord."

As for His words: ﴿And when the earth is stretched out﴾
God, exalted is He, says: and when the earth is spread out and increased in its extent.
Like what was reported:

Scholars of interpretation said similarly to what we have said regarding this.

Those who said so:
